summary:
No criminal provision in Vatican City law reaches consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults in private and non-commercial. The territory's legal code derives from the Italian Zanardelli Code of 1889 and has carried no such offence since 1890, including through the founding of the sovereign state in 1929. Nothing in the criminal law addresses being transgender.

The age of consent is 18 for all persons regardless of gender. A lower age of 14 applies to sexual relations within a marriage recognised as valid by the Catholic Church and by Vatican City law.

Vatican City has no legal mechanism for changing a gender marker on identity documents, and no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity applies in the territory. No rule governs access to single-sex facilities for a trans visitor, and no document-amendment route exists for a resident or a visitor.

Vatican City operates no prison system. It maintains a few cells for pre-trial detention, and a person sentenced to imprisonment by Vatican City serves the term in Italian prisons at Vatican expense. There is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy and no documented case of a trans prisoner held under Vatican City's authority.

The Congregation for Catholic Education's 2019 document 'Male and Female He Created Them' frames 'gender theory' as denying the difference and reciprocity of man and woman and as eliminating the anthropological basis of the family. It is an educational instruction addressed to Catholic institutions rather than a rule binding visitors, but it states the governing institution's position on gender identity.

A 2023 declaration by the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith permitted spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage. A January 2024 press release reiterated that blessings never extend to the unions themselves.

Vatican City has consistently rejected civil recognition of same-sex unions, same-sex marriage, and the granting of adoption rights to same-sex couples. Pope Francis in 2023 expressed support for same-sex civil unions outside the Catholic Church while maintaining that the Sacrament of Marriage is between a man and a woman as instituted by God.

In 2021 Vatican foreign minister Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher wrote to the Italian ambassador to the Holy See objecting to an Italian parliamentary bill meant to protect LGBTQ Italians against violence and discrimination. The objection targeted the provision prohibiting incitement of hatred on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, which the letter described as a violation of freedom of speech and of religion, and asked for the draft law's text to be reformulated.

On 13 January 1998 the activist Alfredo Ormando set himself on fire on St. Peter's Square, under Vatican jurisdiction, in protest at the Catholic religion's refusal of homosexuality. He died days later in hospital from severe burns.
tangentialFactors:
Accreditation rules for foreign diplomats posted to the Holy See bar anyone who is part of a same-sex family and anyone who is divorced. France's openly gay nominee Jean-Loup Kuhn-Delforge, in a civil pact, was rejected in 2008, and the openly gay practising Catholic single nominee Laurent Stefanini was rejected in 2015. France left the post vacant from March 2015 until May 2016 before nominating another diplomat. In October 2008 Catholic officials rejected France's first-choice candidate as ambassador to the Holy See because he is gay, forcing Paris to name a different envoy, a documented instance of the Vatican government refusing an LGBT person in diplomatic relations.

The Holy See's institutional posture against homosexuality and gender theory drives policy in diplomatic and internal matters, while the city-state's own criminal law has not criminalised consensual same-sex conduct in modern times. The legal baseline of the territory and the doctrinal position of the institution that governs it are separate layers.
localsOnly:
The Vatican reserves the right to remove, suspend or dismiss immediately any official or employee who publicly admits to being gay or who questions the general policy of the Vatican towards homosexuals. The provision applies to people working for the governing institutions rather than to visitors.

No anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity applies to residents of Vatican City, and no legal gender recognition procedure exists for them.
outOfScopeNotes:
No United States State Department human rights report chapter for the Holy See exists for 2023 or 2024, so the assessment rests on encyclopedic and institutional sources rather than a government human rights report.

The absence of a documented trans-prisoner placement case reflects the absence of a domestic prison system and of published records, not a finding that no trans person has ever been held in pre-trial detention in Vatican City.

Whether the Vatican's stated right to dismiss officials and employees who publicly acknowledge being gay has been exercised in specific cases is not documented in the sources reviewed.

Enforcement practice at entry, at screening, or in access to facilities for a trans visitor is not documented. No source records a trans visitor being stopped, questioned or refused entry on grounds of gender identity.
